## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed were the flipped states; I noticed that Biden flipped AZ, PA, GA, MI, WI, and a district in NE. The second thing I noticed was the main difference between the 2  maps; the 1st map breaks the states down by the number of electoral votes while the 2nd map shows states, their geographical borders, and how the state voted as a whole. The setup of the 2nd map is a bit misleading. For example, in Nebraska, Trump won the state, but Biden won the 2nd congressional district and 1 out of 5 of Nebraska's electoral college votes. An individual wouldn't be able to gather that information from the second map and would have a false sense of complete unity within each state. Whereas the 1st map highlights the disunity and conflicting views within states. I wonder which map is more commonly published and why. This has a large impact on me personally; I am a senior in high school, so the stance of the party in the White House holds on student loans will have a large impact on my financial situation throughout college and the beginning of my adult life. My community will also feel the impacts of this decision -- both beneficial and harmful. I live in a rural community that has a lack of access to adequate healthcare and the new administration's policy aims to improve that, but my community is also comprised of a majority of farmers, who were greatly dependant upon the subsidies under the Trump administration. Catchy Headline: Is America Red, Blue, or Purple?

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment: From the map of the Electoral College's results, I noticed that Biden flipped in AZ, PA, GA, MI, WI, and one district in NE and flat outwon in VT, NH, MA, NY, NJ, CT, RI, DE, MD, VA, DC, IL, MN, CO, NM, CA, OR, WA, HI, NV, and 3 districts in ME. Trump flat out won ID, MT, ND, SD, WY, UT, IA, KS, AK, OK, TX, MO, AR, LA, AL, MS, FL, NC, SC, WV, TN, KY, IN, OH, four districts from NE and district from ME, flipping in none of the districts. From the state winner map, I noticed that Biden flipped in PA, MI, WI, AZ, GA, and NE 2; he won CA, NV, OR, WA, NM, CO, MN, IL, NY, VA, MD, DE, HI, NJ, CT, RI, MA, VT, NH, and ME 1. Trump flipped in none of the states, but won MT, WY, ID, UT, AK, ND, SD, NE 1 and 3, KS, OK, TX, IA, MO, AR, LA, MS, AL, TN, KY, FL, NC, SC, WV, IN, and OH. I wonder why the northeast, some of the midwest, and west coast voted for Biden and the plains, some of the mid-west, and the south voted Republican? These results impacted my community by raising the chances of a member of the LGBTQ+ community to be hate-crimed and raised the taxes. These maps show the results of the 2020 Presidential Election in the state winner votes and electoral college votes. A catchy headline I would give these maps would be "Donald Trump succeeded from the White House.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
What do I notice? - I notice that the red and blue states are, for the most part, not intermixed with each other. While there are definitely some blue states within the red, those states are always connected to another blue state that is bordering another blue state, etc. I also notice that there are a few blue states that many people did not take as "swing states" that could go blue from red or vice versa.
What do I wonder? - I wonder if those states that swung blue will swing back red next election. I also wonder if there is any way we could continue to intermix ideas to the point that there are several states that "swing" between parties depending on the election and not just 6 in the midwest. 
What impact does this have on me and my community? - Being candid, it doesn't have a ton of impact by itself. People call the POTUS the "most powerful man in the world," on a day to day basis for the American people, the POTUS doesn't have a huge impact. My life under Obama was virtually no different than my life under Trump and realistically looking at all of the communities around the US, the same sentiment will ring true. Personally, I am going into the military, so my life will be directly impacted by the budget proposed by POTUS and the actions that he takes when it comes to foreign policy, but I am not the average American.
Write a catchy headline - "25 to 25 - Why the States' 'Tie' Ended in Victory for Biden"

raw_comment:
#1) When looking at the map I first noticed that the electoral votes are clearly recorded at the top of both maps. At first glance, it would appear that there is a higher number of red states than blue states. However, through further analysis and outside research, one can see that the areas that are predominantly red tend to be states comprised primarily of rural, white communities with smaller populations, and fewer electoral votes ( since the number of votes per state is proportional to each state's population). While the blue states are primarily comprised of larger diverse communities with more electoral votes. 

#2) I wonder why the first map is not publicized as widely as the second map. The first map allows for a simplified explanation of the electoral votes, which, in turn, allows for greater accessibility to a wide range of people across the country. 

#3) This impacts everyone in my community, and around the world because of the power that the president of the United States holds—the power to make potentially life-altering decisions for millions of people. These maps will help to educate Americans on the political system that holds millions of lives in its grasp. 

#4) Headline: “Confused how electoral votes work? Check out this simplified map.”

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment: I notice that the first graph displays little boxes representing each electoral vote each state gets. I also notice that in the first graph, some states have different colors within them. This indicates that some of their votes went to one candidate, and some of their votes went to the other. On both graphs, the states that flipped are colored darker and have stripes on them. Both maps display the 2020 election results. I wonder why the second map is the one we see more often, as it is more misleading than the former map. The second map looks to be all red, but when you think of how many votes the red states in the midwest get, it truly isn't a lot of red. The states in the midwest are less populated than the blue states, so it is completely misleading to assume Trump won solely based on the states he had. This has a large impact on my community. I live in California, which is a major democratic state, but this map can be misleading for those who do support Trump in my area. A catchy title for this all would be: Land or Population? 2020 Election Results.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that both of these maps show the results of the election in different ways. The first one shows the map of the United States, but each state is represented by pixels in how many EC votes that state has. The second map is just the normal US map with each state colored with the candidate called for that state. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the top map isn’t used more often, since many people use the argument of “you see the map is mostly red” to say trump won the election. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This affects everyone. Helping everyone understand how the election works and that this election was fair and not rigged may reduce the amount of hostility around the election.

Don’t Understand How the Electoral College Works? This Map Breaks It Down.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

A president can incite unity, yet also fuel division and this national temperament effects us all.

raw_comment: I notice that both maps display the 2020 election results, but the first map does so more accurately. In the first map, each state is depicted by the number of electoral votes, one block representing one vote. The second map shows the states’ actual sizes which are colored to represent whoever won that state. In the second map, it falsely suggests that bigger states carry more weight in the election which is why Trump appears to be leading. By completely ignoring the electoral vote, it does not consider the weight each states’ votes have accounting for their population, as the first map does. Oklahoma is much larger than Connecticut on the second map when in reality, they have the same amount of electoral votes. I wonder why the second map is what we most commonly see during elections? It can be very misleading as it does not account for smaller states with higher populations, which in this case are the majority of what Biden won. I also wonder why Nebraska and Maine have split electoral votes? I’m curious what the advantage is of doing this is instead of using winner takes all like every other state. This has an impact on my community and me because New Hampshire is a geographically small state. The first map reveals that our votes may be weighted more than we realize, every vote does count. NH has only one less electoral vote than Colorado, which appears much larger on the second map. My headline is: “Are the Maps We Usually See as Accurate as We’ve Been Led To Believe?"

raw_comment: I noticed that the first map more clearly displays how the votes are split between Biden and Trump. On the 2nd map, which is more traditionally used for things like the news, at first glance it seems like Trump should have won. On the 1st map, you see how some of the states for Biden account for a lot more than some of the small states that are for Trump. I wonder why we stick to the 2nd style of map. We don't have to turn all the way to the craziness that is the first map, but it would be a lot clearer if there was some indication of how many votes each state gives to their candidate. This affect my community because I think the 2nd map can be misleading. Some of people have been insinuating that the voting is rigged, or that the government cheated in Biden's favor. Most people have these opinions because of voter fraud, but it's likely that some see the 2nd map and think that Trump clearly won, so were shocked to see that Biden ended up winning.

1. At first glance I notice that the 1st graph seems to be a lot more accurate than the 2nd one, the 2nd is a bit misleading based on the fact that there is so much red but Donald Trump didn’t win. The 2nd graph’s name could be: “A look on which candidate dominated in all states”.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

On the night of the election, President Trump was leading several key states namely; Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona, and Georgia. What do you wonder?
Would the election have turned out differently if every vote was finalized and counted on the night of the election. 

What impact does this have on your community?
At the end of the day whatever happens, happens for a reason. We just have to make the best if it.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the first graph displays a more accurate depiction of how the states actually voted. Take Nebraska for example. You can see there is a little bit of blue, which means it wasn't entirely dominated by Republican votes.
2. I wonder if these statistics would be any different if everyone over 18 voted. There were many non-voters. Would the results be more blue or red if they did?
3. I live in a very dark blue area in Ohio (northeast). These graphs may show which vote swept the state, but not the heavily populated areas in Midwestern states which normally lean to the right. Even though I'm in a very liberal community, the country will still see Ohio as a very conservative state. 
4. I would title the first graph: "Evidence of a fair election; dark blue dominates fair and square."

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice how the two maps are different from each other, like on the second map of the states there seems to be more red than blue, which than makes others question who really won the election but when you look at the first map that shows the college of electoral votes it’s more clear to seeing who won the election.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how many states had a second thought about their votes?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
One impact this has on the community and myself is that the second map supports one side and the electoral map supports the claim of the other controversial side.

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.

One graph represents the red team as having more votes, while the other graph represents more of the blue teams votes having an increase. - **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:

  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?  The first map shows that Biden is winning overall. He has the most votes from states on the west coast and in the northeast. The second map also shows Biden winning, but when you look at it by state, it appears Trump has more votes. This is because the population in many of the blue states is larger so they get more electoral votes. 
2.  What do you wonder? It's interesting that states on the coasts are more democratic than states in the middle of the country. It makes me wonder how much population relates to the political parties.
3. What impact does this have on you and your community? This shows that certain states have more influence when it comes to the election. For example, Ohio has 18 electoral votes, which makes our influence about average. Ohio used to be a swing state, but now it appears to be more Republican, which might affect future elections.
4. What's going on in this graph? These graphs show that votes are based on population, and states that have larger land areas can still have a small number of electoral votes. The first map helps show the actual division of the votes, which is helpful because sometimes it is hard to comprehend. A headline: The Electoral College Map Shows that Big States Might not Have Such a Big Impact.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
1. Firstly, I notice that states on the coast are largely blue. This makes sense, as coastal areas tend to be more urban, and urban areas tend to vote democratic. I also notice Nebraska and Maine- the only states without a policy which gives the state's winner all of its electoral votes. 
2. I wonder how the first map would look if electoral votes were decided in a different way, a proportional representation of how people in that state actually voted, and if that way might be more fair. 
3. This process affects me and everyone in my community greatly, because it decides who the president is. We need to make sure the procedures surrounding this important election are fair and representative of everybody. For example, Ohio gave all of its votes to Donald Trump- but over 45% of Ohioans voted for Joe Biden. In applying this "winner-take-all" mentality to what is often a hair's difference does not create a picture that accurately represents America. 
4. "Winner-Take-All Presidential Policy Silences Millions Of Voters"

raw_comment:
Headline: Like Tetris, ‘Merica’s votes are crashing into place. 

Noticed: These maps show how, overall, there are certain trends of voting depending on where you live.  If you live in more rural areas, then you will likely vote republican, and if you live in urban areas, then you will likely vote democrat.  I also think that Wis., Arz., Ga., Pa., and Mich. are all states that were fought over intensely, as they all flipped their votes.  I think it is interesting that there are no red flipped states, potentially showing how the Republican party was dominant in such areas.

Wonder:
I wonder what would happen if you changed the electoral votes to based on the size of the state. I think that it would be interesting because it would be different. I also think that if the states were judged based on size, Trump would have won because he has the rural places. I wonder what the maps would look like if fewer states had the winner take all rule. I also wonder how much the results would change. 


Impacts: 
What impact does this have on you and your community?
I think that this will affect my community by putting a lot of stress on my family and friends. This would put stress on my peeps because this matters a lot and will affect us for the next four years.

1. I notice that both of these graphs are of the results of this years presidential election but have different ways of displaying the data. I notice the first graph shows who won electoral votes demonstrated by colored boxes (each box corresponding to one electoral vote). The second graph isn't not straight forward and is harder to read because it shows what party the state voted for but not the numbers of people or electoral votes. The first graph shows more blue which would accurately represent the results considering Biden won and is marked by blue. 
2. I wonder why the second graph is more widely used when showing election data but is not as accurate. It doesn't correctly display the results of each state which could mislead people.
3. The impact this had on my community was that it shows New Hampshire having all four electoral votes blue meaning we voted democratic. I hope that we continue to vote like this in further elections. 
4. The graphs are displaying the 2020 presidential election results in two different ways. 
"Behind the scenes"

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
1. I notice that some typically republican voting states voted in favor of the democratic candidate this year. This is a major shift for this election, but it also provides insight as to what states really are "swing states." At this point in the country's life, Ohio no longer seems to be a swing state.
2. I wonder how I did not see the first map displayed instead of the first when the election was occurring. I was not aware of a more detailed/streamlined map to better understand the outcome of the election. Was it perhaps not advertised as much?
3. The outcome of the election has a severe impact on my community. With Biden becoming victorious, he has promised fast and strict regulation of the coronavirus, and if he follows through on this promise, lots of local businesses could cease to exist (but this comes at the important caveat that the pandemic could be over sooner than later).
4. "Biden ‘Trumps’ Donald Trump in Presidential Election”

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |

| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment: I notice that the first graph isolates each state by the votes from the Electoral College. States that appear to be big in size can become much smaller and vice versa. In the second graph, it seems as though the majority vote is for Donald Trump because most states are red. For example, the Electoral College wouldn't matter and the population would be the important asset in counting the votes. ## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
- I notice that at first glance, the bottom map appears to look like red is the majority and therefore should win, while the top map shows a more split map with a slight majority being blue and therefore blue should win. The red dominates the rural areas while blue is stronger on the coasts and in more metropolitan areas. 
- I wonder how two maps showing the same result can look so different. It is deceiving at first, but when analyzed it is clear to see that large states do not directly correlate with a large population, and therefore a large number of electoral votes.
- This has an impact on my community because with today's politics being so polarized, the deception of the map may cause more of an outrage; especially since the electoral college is misunderstood by many Americans. 
- A possible title could be: Polarizing Deceptions in American Politics

- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.

  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.

- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:

  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,

  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
1. Both graphs give the same details of which states won what party, but the first graph gets more in detail than the second graph as it shows how many exact electoral votes each state has, the divide in the votes from Nebraska and Maine. Looking aside from the differences, the divide in parties from both maps shown has the blue more in the upper right area or New England area of the US and the west coast, while the country is more red around the central areas of the US.
2. I wonder why we have this type of divide in parties in these specific areas, as the majorities of red and blue states seem to be common in each election in the areas that I described them in.
3. The impact on these decisions with each state on myself and my community is the fact that it decides who the President is, the person that looks over the entire US. He has an important role in this higher-up position, and the decision of who it is is very important for the future of our nation.
4. The headline that I would do would be  “Electoral Voting: Winning Does Not Take Claiming The Most States."

raw_comment:
Both graphs show whether the state was won or flipped. However, I noticed that the first graph is more detailed than the second graph. The first graph shows the number of electoral votes per state and whether each individual vote was a win or was flipped. This depicts the election results better as the second map could mislead others since Trump won more states than Biden yet Biden still had the greater number of votes. I noticed that many of the flip states are blue. Many of the central states are red, while states in the New England area and West Coast are blue. 

 I wonder why we tend to see graphs like the second which provides a more general overview rather than graphs like the first which provides more detail. I also wonder why Maine and Nebraska are the only states with split electoral votes. I wonder how the environment, culture, and lifestyle of each state affects the views of voters and the candidate that they end up voting for. I also wonder how this year's election graphs compare to those of past elections. 

This impacts me and my community because it impacts the whole nation. The president plays an important role in our federal system. In addition, many people don't fully understand the Electoral College and how votes are secured. Massachusetts is known to be a democratic and blue state, so it's interesting to see how other states fall in the political spectrum. 

A headline could be "Breaking Down the Election: Understanding the Electoral College."
