## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
I notice that in the first graph, each grid box in a state represents an electoral vote, while the second graph does not have any symbol for the electoral votes. This makes the first one easier for me to interpret. I see that even though Biden won, the second graph makes me think that Trump must have gotten more votes due to the sea of red. I find it funny that even though the two candidates won the same number of states (with Biden getting the District of Columbia), in the second graph it looks like Trump has won many more states.
I wonder what other types of graphs are being used to represent the 2020 election. Are there any other more effective types of graphs? I also wonder, on a side note, why many conservatives are sure that Trump has won when Biden clearly received more electoral votes according to both of these graphs.
This has a huge impact on me and my community. Who wins this election will determine whether we get out of this pandemic and whether our economy remains as good as it has been in the past four years. Both candidates could have brought good things to the table, but Biden winning will allow us to have a president who will enforce the vaccination when it is created.
My title would be "Clear Winner? Biden wins with a higher number of votes, states, and electors."

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice that the first map is organized by electoral votes, providing a proportional representation of electorate distribution corresponding to the actual results of the election, showing a clear victory for Biden, whereas the second map is simply shaded in by land area, making the country appear disproportionately red. Additionally, I noticed that 5 states appear to have learned from their mistakes in 2016 and flipped. I noticed as well that the 10 most educated states voted for Biden, while the 7 least educated states voted for Trump.

What do you wonder?

I wonder if the electoral college is a fair system, or if it’s outdated due to drastic differences in circumstance from the 1700s to today. The system was created to prevent a tyrannical majority from dominating rural areas, however it seems to be that a lot of bigots are exploiting this system and targeting marginalized communities throughout the country against the wishes of a majority of Americans as can be seen by the 2016 popular vote.

What impact does this have on you and your community?

As a small state, New Hampshire is given disproportionate representation when it comes to electorate votes, and the layout shows how a NH vote has more than twice the value of a vote in CA.

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.

“Some mistakes are made, that’s alright, that's ok: 5 states learn from their mistakes and turn blue, securing Biden’s victory.”

raw_comment: I notice that Utah is the only state in the four corners that voted for Trump I notice that the majority of New England (except for a region in Maine) voted for Biden. The entire North coast except for Alaska had a majority of voters vote for Biden. The western states not on the coast and the entire western edge of the midwest primarily voted for Trump, with only Colorado, and Arizona had the majority vote for Biden. I notice that most of the southeast voted for Trump except for a small group including Georgia, Virginia, Maryland, D.C., and Delaware. I notice that most states near large bodies of water (such as The Great Lakes, The Pacific Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean) voted for Biden, with only a few exceptions (Alaska, Florida, North Carolina, a small portion of Maine, and South Carolina). I notice that all of the states that voted for Trump were touching eachother (except for Alaska which touches no other states). I notice that even though the majority of states voted for Trump, Biden had more votes from the electoral college. I wonder what the average difference between Trump and Biden voters is in states that voted republican versus those who voted democratically. A possible title for this graph would be "Where does your state stand on this years election".

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment: In this weeks graph, it shows two different forms of maps representing the same topic. I see certain areas in the US vote republican while others vote democratic. I also notice that it shows the election winning and which state voted for which candidate. The first graph with spaced out states showing the places that voted is the better graph to look at. Even though it's not as easy to look at, it better demonstrates the electoral votes for each state and which candidate won the state. The votes are counted based on the electoral college and it's more important to look at the graph by votes as they add up rather than looking at it as a whole. I wonder why particular areas in our country vote for a certain candidate rather than the votes in each state being all scattered around the states. This has an impact on my community because either could win and it could be flipped in the next election. Even one big city in a state can take over the votes and change the candidate. My headline would be "The 2020 Election Map."

raw_comment: From looking at the maps, I noticed that they are both very similar to each other in many ways. I believe that the overall idea of the graph is to show which presidential candidate in the 2020 election won each state. The one difference between the maps that I noticed however, was that the second one is a map of the United States with state borders, while the first one shows the states individually spaced out around where they normally would be on a map. So basically, the first map shows the same information as the second one, just in a more spread out view. I wonder why someone would want to make the first map, or even analyze it, because to me the second map is a much better representation of what is trying to be shown since we are more familiar with looking at normal maps of the world. Another thing that I am confused about on the second map, is that there is both red and blue in the states of Maine and Nebraska. I am not sure what that means. Overall the graph shows which states each presidential candidate won in the 2020 election. I think that a good headline for the graph would be “How the United States Voted in the 2020 Presidential Election by State”

raw_comment: This is a map that people all around the world and from different countries are familiar with. As an American, I can find myself checking these maps daily to see if anything has changed with the 2020 presidential election. I have noticed that many of the central states are in favor of the Republican party. I also noticed that some of the coastal states favor the Democratic side. One thing that I have found interesting is that there are 5 states that are blue but have lines over them. I Know that these states have been flipped because in the last election they were Republican. I believe that these states have played a major role in the election and the votes could have swayed either way. This has an impact on my community because I live in a big county that I feel could have determined if Wisconsin was red or blue. There are a lot of people that live here and I feel like one county or city can determine the outcome. I think we should have a map that shows each city, therefore, there can be a straightforward and honest answer.

raw_comment:
-What do you notice?:
In the second graph, without any prior knowledge as to how U.S elections work, it would appear as though Donald Trump won. We on the other hand, know that this is not the case and although there are more red states than blue, with the understanding of the electoral college we can deduce that Joe Biden was the winner. I also notice how the first graph is broken down into electoral college votes from each state, making it clearer and easier to see how it is that Joe Biden won this election.
   -What do you wonder?:
One of the main wonderings I have about these graphs, and the way U.S elections are run in the first place, is why certain states have long standing histories of voting for a certain party, while there are others we classify as ‘swing states’. What is it that causes these distinctions to happen and why are they so consistent?
   -What impact does this have on you and your community?:
I feel as though the impact this has on me and my community is more widespread than meets the eye. If every U.S citizen a look at some of the proven information about the election I believe that there would be less conflict and argument over what is factual information and what is “fake news” per se. 
   -Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea:
“A Deeper Look into the 2020 Presidential Election Maps”

raw_comment:
I notice that more of the central states are voting Trump than the outer states, and none of the red states could flip. I notice that quite a few of the blue states are swing/flip states as well. 

I wonder why there are less blue states than red, yet Biden is still in the lead. Could this be that those states have the majority of the electoral colleges, and therefore have the majority of the votes. 

I think that this impacts my community by showing people that more states are red, with could lead them to believe that there was voter fraud, since there is no number of how many electoral colleges there are in each state. I think this is a common misleading problem.

My headline is: "Red or Blue? Biden wins over the coastal states."

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Land Doesn’t Vote, People Do” by Sophia of New Hampshire and by Matthew of Ohio; “The Truth Behind Election Maps” by Jackson of New Hampshire; “Accurate Electoral Map Shows Biden Got More Votes Than You Might Think” by Aidan of Ohio; and two Red/Blue headlines -- “America’s Red or Blue Future.” by Kayshaleen of Massachusetts, and “Blue or Red, Biden Is The Ultimate Winner On These Maps” by Sarah from Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, New Jersey.
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Dec. 4 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the maps, and a few Stat Nuggets.
 
Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or
a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs). 
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who thinks these maps show why the use of the Electoral College to select the President should be reevaluated, and Ben Kirk of Ithaca, New York, who thinks a picture, or an electoral college map of the US, is worth a thousand words!

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |

| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
Looking at this graph I notice that these are the results from the 2020 presidential election. The first graph divides the states up into boxes that represent the number of electoral college votes. I notice that on this graph blue and red-colored states, but also a few navy blue states. Looking at the map it seems as though there are many more red states, but the bar on the top clearly states that Joe Biden won. I wonder why there aren't any really dark red states whereas there are some really dark blue states? I wonder why the news does not display the first map during the election? I feel like that would be a very helpful graph that people could easily understand and it could benefit not only my community but also the nation. This could also impact my community as each graph clearly displays what candidate my state voted for. 

Title: "Presidential Election of 2020"

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
In looking at these graphs, it is very clear which one does a better job at visualizing the outcome of the election. The first graph shows which party each state voted for as well as how many electoral college members from each state had a say. By seeing this, it allows the audience to understand why Biden won. From looking at these graphs I notice that most mid west and southern states learn more  right whereas the west coast and north east lean more left. I wonder why that is and if the lifestyle and culture in those states contribute to the winning party in each state. This impacts my community because New Jersey is a very densely populated state yet normally always leans left. Because of this, I wonder how many Republicans vs Democrats are in the state of NJ. 
A catchy headline would be, "A Closer Look Into This Years Election"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the top map shows the states broken up and made up of individual squares that represent how many electoral votes each winner of the state got. The bottom map shows the states together and just shows each states winner. Both maps differentiate Biden and Trump by blue and red, and also show flip states by striped lines. I also noticed that both maps show that most Trump supporters are in the middle states while Biden supporters seem to be mostly on the coasts. Lastly, I realized that most people focus on the bottom map rather then the electoral  map when looking at who won.

What do you wonder?
I wonder what makes the west and east coast support Biden rather then Trump. Vice versa, I wonder what makes the middle states more prone to supporting Trump. What does the environment have to do with who you support? I wonder this because environment does seem to influence which candidate won in the state. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts my community as an American in understanding the importance of looking at both electoral votes as well as overall votes in each state, and how this influences who won. It also impacts my community because living in the east coast it is interesting to see how almost all east coast states voted blue in the electoral map and overall map. 

A headline for this graph can be "Blue or Red, Biden Is The Ultimate Winner On These Maps"

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

What do you notice?
Even though, on the first day of election day, the number between the two candidates are close, the two graphs here shows how undeniable Biden wins as he has 74 more electoral votes compare to Trump.   - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
What do you notice: I noticed in the states which adopted a congressional district model of electoral voting, one elector voted against the consensus of the rest of the state electors' votes. In both Maine and Nebraska, it was their second district, but for different parties. Maine's 2nd district contains a majority of their rural land (accounting for their red vote) whilst Nebraska's second district contains Omaha, the largest city in the state (accounting for the blue vote).

What do you wonder: Is the electoral system really fair in its current state? Is it fair at all? Does it make sense that land should have a higher say in the leadership of the nation? In a nation as large and with needs as separate as ours, does it make sense to perpetuate the system which sees the election of one national figurehead? A state could have a near perfectly split popular vote yet those few votes could decide the entire say of that given state. 

What impact does this have on you and your community: This map really hammers home the importance of voting and making our voices be heard. As a community, we HAVE to make our opinions known to the national stage and the most surefire way to do so is to vote. 

What’s going on in this graph: This graph shows the shifting opinions of the nation since the last election and displays the various wants and needs of the people who voted in their respective regions. A potential headline could be: "Separate Needs, Seperate Worlds: A nation fragmented".

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment: I notice that the first map shows each state by how many electoral votes it has, while also taking partial form of what the state looks like. I also notice that states that give electoral votes based on the counties's popular vote, for example Nebraska and Maine, have one electoral vote shaded as the other candidate. I think that the first map takes some time getting used to, but I like how it looks abstract and different, and it shows how many electoral votes states each get, and I notice that it shows their impact on the election, and elections to come. I wonder why certain states have the population that they have. For instance, why do so many people live in California? I think a catchy name for this graph would be President Elect Joe Biden has won the election, but which states/electoral did he win?

WHAT DO YOU NOTICE?
I notice that there are not many states that have split colors, meaning that the state is usually all blue or all red, not mostly red with one blue or vise versa.

I also wonder why on the second map some of the blue states are darker than others. Why are they there and why is there not any on the red ones?

A Political Map No One Has Ever Seen

raw_comment: I notice that the two different maps show two different things. The top one, which I believe is a better map, shows the electoral votes that each state has, as well as who had more votes in that state, whereas the bottom map only shows who had more votes in each state, with no depiction of how many electoral votes each state has. I wonder why most maps that I see don't show the electoral votes, but only the states, like the bottom map. I feel that the top map is a much better depiction of who is currently winning the election. These maps impact me and my community because I feel like a lot of times, kids that are my age can't really fathom what the electoral college is, so the top map really gives people my age a good idea of what the electoral college is and how it works. For instance, when I was talking to one of my friends about the election, they said that if there wasn't a bar on the top of the map showing who was winning, they would think that the Republican was winning, although, in reality, it's the Democrat. In conclusion, I feel that the top map gives people a better idea of not only how the electoral college works, but who is truly winning the election, and why, even though the Republican had more states' popular vote, the Democrat actually was winning.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the top map depicts each electoral vote, while the bottom map depicts the election results of each state. I notice that the top map is never usually put out into the media. I have only seen maps such as the bottom one on the news or on social media. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why maps like the top one are not popular. I believe the top map does a better job of offering a visual of the election results. The top map also highlights one of the flaws of the electoral college; there is no guarantee that electoral voters will vote according to the results of their state. One of the five electoral voters in Nebraska voted blue, even though the popular vote in Nebraska indicated that all the votes should have gone to Donald Trump. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
A lot of students my age do not fully understand the electoral college. I believe the first map helps explain what the electoral college system actually is. Therefore, these maps have  the power to educate my community.

raw_comment:
I notice that the top map represents every elector in the electoral college, so a state's size is just based on their electoral votes. In the bottom map, it is the United States as usually shown, with each state colored by the party that won. In the top, it looks much more blue, while the bottom looks more red. This shows that the most important thing isn't land mass, it's electoral votes. 

I wonder why more states haven't divided their electoral votes to make it not a winner-take-all system. 

This map impacts me because it shows me how a candidate can win even though in a map by landmass it looks like they lost.

raw_comment:
Looking at the first map, I noticed that every box used to show the states was equal to the amount of electoral college votes. This map also shows the split states together. In the second map however, maps are given to the party where majority of the electoral college votes were given, with split states moved to the side, making the vocal point of the map read as the block of red through the map. 
I wonder about who was making the different graphs and if there was any impact because of personal beliefs, even when representing the same numbers. 
The impact of these maps show the difference in the systems that the country looks to, comparing land mass to the electoral college ,and the difference viewers might see. In my community, it shows the impact blue cities have on surrounding red counties. 
A possible headline could be "Sizable Differences: A Tale of Two Maps"

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the top map is spaced out in such a way that expresses how the population of each state is expressed through votes. By spreading the states apart and adjusting the sizes, the map reads in a way that Biden has a more dominant lead over Trump. The states are sized in this specific way to show the number of electoral votes each state has, so although they maybe are shaped like their formation, there is no true correlation to their size. By having the states all connect in the second graph, it appears as if Trump maintains the lead. However, this has no true correspondence with a population per state. 

2. I primarily wonder why maps such as the first one are not used as much in mass media. This is because the first map thoroughly describes the true votes based on electors and such. When using the map that shows electoral votes, it is viewed as more accurate. 

3. This impacts me and my community because it shows how despite being a small state, we have very similar amounts of electoral votes when compared to other larger states. This only proves how important the population plays a role in voting.

4. The first map breaks down the electoral votes per each state and which way they swayed and the second map depicts the states based on their regular size without mentioning electoral votes, and also shows which way they swayed. If I were to write a title for this article it would be “The true role of electoral votes.”

raw_comment:
I notice the first map does a better job at visualizing the outcome of the 2020 presidential election. If you look at the second map you see an overwhelming amount of red states which could lead an individual to thinking the Republican Party and Donald Trump won. However, the second map shows more clearly the number of electoral votes each state has and makes it easier to tell how Joe Biden won with the votes he's got.

I wonder would more people vote if America abolished the electoral college system? If you have identify with the Republican Party but live in CA (and other examples like that), do some voters not even vote because they know their vote won't be heard? Even people who are in the middle of the political spectrum and aren't sure who to vote for may not vote if they live in a state that is heavily republican or democrat.

This impacts my community and I because the winner of the election, Joe Biden, will lead our country for the next four, potentially eight, years. Especially with COVID-19 numbers at an all time high and the civil unrest, how the new leader reacts and the actions he takes will have a major effect on how life will continue for my fellow Americans.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
1.) What do you notice?
	The first graph shows the states with their number of electoral votes. The second map is a typical geographic map of the states. The first map appears bluer, while the second looks redder. The states look more proportional in the first map. 

2.)What do you wonder?
Why not use the first map? it makes the electoral college easier to understand and easier to see visually. Why do we do it this way? this makes no sense. 

3.)What impact does this have on you and your community?
	I feel like this is something I already kind of knew so it did not affect me very much, but I imagine it would shock quite a few members of my community. Most people do not understand just how off our map looks compared to the first one which is a more accurate visual.

4.)What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.
Truth Vs. Trump.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  
Today’s maps show the 2020 Presidential election results in two different ways.  Compare the maps.  How are they similar?  How are they different?  Which map does a better job of visualizing the outcome of the election?  
Share your noticings and wonderings with others.  Together, you will come up with a better understanding of the story that these graphs tell.
From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the map. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this map and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next release will be by Friday, Dec. 4 with moderation on Wednesday, Dec. 9.  The graph is about how the United States compares to countries worldwide.

raw_comment:
The second map is much more misleading than the second map because it would appear that the majority of the states are red and therefore Trump should have won. This however is incorrect and why the first map more accurately displays the 2020 election. The first map has each block represent one electoral vote, and shows how the votes were distributed in the 2020 election. It incorporates not only which states voted for which candidate but also the number of electoral votes for each state. 

I wonder why Maine and Nebraska each have split electoral votes. I also wonder why the second map is so much more common when it is quite misleading. I think that it would be smarter to use the first map more often because it seems to give a better perspective on who won the election. There might be a reason why the second map is more common, so I wonder what that reason is.

The first map shows each state with the electoral college votes by winner, while the second map just shows each state’s winner. A headline for the graphs would be “The 2020 Election: Electoral Votes vs. Land Mass”.

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:

  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the first graph shows electoral votes in boxes, with each box being one of the states electoral votes. This makes it possible to see how much each state actually affected the election. The second graph shows what party the state voted for, making it a little misleading considering it shows the state size, not electoral votes or number of actual voters in the state. The first graph consists of more blue, which is the actual result of the election, while the second graph shows more red.

2. I wonder why the second graph is more commonly shown considering it can definitely throw people off just like it did this election when some accused Biden supporters of cheating.

3. These graphs affect my community because New Hampshire tends to be a swing state. This year it swung blue, helping Biden win the election. It also affects my community because most of the states in the north-east tend to vote blue, becoming a big part of the democratic win. 

4. These graphs show the 2020 election in two different ways, electoral votes, and which party won the state, the second way more misleading.

State size doesn’t equal amount of votes

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
I notice that the first graph shows each state by the number of electoral votes they have in the election, while the second map shows each state geographically and whether they sided blue or red. On the first map each individual box represents one electoral vote. The second map is more commonly seen and is shown when data about presidential elections is talked about on the news. Overall, the first map gives us a much more accurate representation of the election outcome because it shows us the specific number of electoral votes each state has, and when added up, Joe Biden has quite a few more votes than Donald Trump.

I wonder why Maine and Nebraska don’t have the “winner takes all” policy like every other US state, and are allowed to split their electoral votes by not having to go one way or the other. 

This has an impact on my community and I because since New Hampshire only has four electoral votes it is crucial that everyone who is eligible to vote, does. Even though our state’s population is small compared to others, our four electoral votes are still very important and could possibly be a tie breaker or help a presidential candidate reach 270 votes. 

The presidential election results in the first map are represented by the number of electoral votes each state has, and the second map just shows which candidate won each state. A catchy headline that I thought of to represent both maps is “Don’t always judge a map by its cover.”

raw_comment: The first thing I notice from these maps is how the change in how the data is displayed makes a big difference in interpreting the data. In the top map, the states are represented based on their electoral votes, making it appear that Biden received more votes, which is accurate. In the bottom map, states are colored by which candidate won them overall, making it appear as if Trump won more of the country. This is misleading because the areas that Trump won are less populated than where Biden won, leading to Biden's win. I wonder how people working in the polling industry use the displaying of data to guide the population to one belief or another. I find it interesting but worrying that people who make political maps can use the human eye to make people believe something that isn’t true. This is the impact that these maps have on my community: we all see things every day that are misleading, but we often believe these things anyway. I hope that non-misleading forms of visual data will become more widely used so that data presented to the public does not come with forms of bias. In terms of what is going on in each map, they both represent two very different things. For the top map, I would title this one “Which Candidate Won the Majority of Electoral Votes?." I would title the bottom map “The 2020 Presidential Candidate That Won Each State,” as this map does not break the states down into a respective size based on the number of electoral votes.

raw_comment:
1.) What do you notice?
	The first graph displays the states with the number of their electoral votes; the states have space between their borders. The second map is a typical geographic map of the states. The states vary in size from the second map due to the number of electoral votes. The first map shows that most of the votes were for Biden. The second map makes the results appear as if Trump had more votes.

2.)What do you wonder?
Why do we use the second map more often when the first is clearly more accurate? The size of the states on the first map is based on their number of electoral votes; this more accurately demonstrates the outcome of the election because of how it is oriented. Some people may make assumptions based on the size of a state rather than their number of electoral votes, which can lead to accusations and controversies. 

3.)What impact does this have on you and your community?
	I will definitely look at maps like this differently now that I’ve seen a new demonstration. I know if others in my community saw this, they would be shocked and may be more likely to do more research on the election process. Perhaps seeing that the typical election map is inaccurate will lead to others seeking a better education.

4.)What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.
	“Square do we draw the line?”

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
I notice that the size of states in the first map is not to scale. For example, Alaska is clearly larger than New Hampshire, however, on the first map, New Hampshire has one more electoral vote compared to Alaska. This clearly depicts how the electoral votes are determined by population size, rather than landmass. I notice that though the states on the second map look more like a typical geographic map when you count the states it seems like Donald Trump is winning the election. If a viewer does not see the electoral vote count at the top of the map, they might believe incorrectly believe that Donald Trump is winning the election, which is not true. 
I wonder why news castings and websites do not typically show the first map. The first map makes a clear distinction about who was winning based. The second map can be misleading because people tend to look at the map and judge the winner based on the area that each color takes up.
This impacts my community because though we have a Republican governor, we still elected Joe Biden as a whole. This shows how we elect our representatives based on opinion on policies and promises instead of on what party each candidate is from.
 When looking at the first map, you can clearly see the length of Joe Biden’s victory. The second map is misleading because it seems that Donald Trump is winning the election, whereas the truth is quite the opposite. A catchy headline may be, “Populations vs. Area”

raw_comment:
1)I noticed in the first map, it did a good job of showing a somewhat even distribution of both parties across America, whereas, in the second map, It would be very easy for someone to look at it and assume that the republican party won just seeing the vast area in the midwest. So even though Biden won, the second map can deceive some by the looks.
2) I always wondered why some states time and time again strictly just vote for one party. In my opinion, every state should be a swing state or just vote for the obviously better-fit person to lead the country. I also wonder why there aren’t more colors seen on the maps. Third parties aren’t even given a chance since everyone is forced to pick a side just to see the other party not win. Almost every election time the map for the most part looks like the second one, and I believe people would benefit more to gain a better understanding by looking at the first map.
	3)While the majority of people in a country mostly get to elect their leader, there will always be the people who are in the minority who just won't accept that most people don’t support their opinion. This can create a division among people and communities when about 55-60% of votes go towards the majority, but then leaving those 40-45% of people either upset or feel as if it should’ve gone their way. People get so tense about party affiliations nowadays so that now there finally is someone chosen, everyone is now starting to calm down. 
4)“The people vs. the land”

raw_comment:
1)
I noticed that the first map shows the states by the number of electoral votes they had. Each state is made of blocks where each block represents an electoral vote. The second of the two maps I noticed was just a classic map of the US. Each state was filled in by color to show which candidate won. However, the second map did not show how many electoral votes each state was worth. The second map could be seen as misleading as Maine appears larger than CT and could cause some to believe it has more sway than CT. This problem does not occur in the first map

2)
I wonder why the second map is more popular when it clearly is inferior to the first. The first map gives a more clear representation of what actually happened in the election as it shows each state by electoral power, not size. I also wonder what it would take to make a nationwide switch to the first map and why we have not already. 

3)
This has an impact on my community as I live in New Hampshire. As New Hampshire has a pretty low population we do not have many electoral votes. The first map is a better representation of what sway we have over the election. Therefore, the use of the second could make some believe that we have more sway than we do. 

4)
The first of the two maps shows the election results based on electoral votes. The second shows who won the state without taking into account the number of electoral votes the state has. A possible catchy headline could be “Electoral Votes Win Out."

raw_comment:
1.) I notice that though both graphs share the same data, they are displayed in different ways. The bottom graph is the standard election map which appears more red than blue, however, the first graph shows states by how many electoral votes they offer and who they went to. These graphs though containing the same data, display it much differently. I believe that the top graph is more effective for a viewer as it is a more accurate representation of who got more votes. 
2.) I wonder why the top graph isn’t used more in the mainstream media. I believe that the system for voting in America, though not flawed, seems to be more complicated than it needs to. I would imagine that along with confusion around the electoral college itself, many people might be confused at how Biden won the election, as when looking at the bottom map it appears America is majority red. I wonder why they don’t switch to the top graph on mainstream media, as I feel that would aid confusion in voters and citizens.
3.) This graph helps people understand how voting works in America, and how different population sizes throughout states affect the number of electoral votes your state offers.
4.) These graphs display the outcome of the 2020 presidential election in two different ways. The first graph shows which states voted for who based on the number of electoral votes they offer, while the second graph shows simply which states voted for who. Catchy Headline “The Truth Behind Election Maps”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the first graph is visualized using blocks. The number of blocks for each state represents the number of electoral votes. I also noticed that Maine has one red block and three blue blocks and Nebraska has one blue block and four red blocks. I noticed that the second graph is a map of the United States. The states are colored red or blue based on the popular vote for the entire state. I also noticed in the key there is a blue and red box labeled Maine 1 and Maine 2 to show the one republican electoral vote in the state. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the second map that shows each state by majority vote is used more when the first map that shows the electoral votes is the most important?
Do people realize the misinterpretation that is caused by the second graph?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
My community and I can easily understand which states are more important than others in the first graph. The second graph impacts my community and I by creating a misinterpretation based on the majority of the red color, when the Democrats got more electoral votes. Overall, both graphs show the importance of everyone voting.


What’s Going on in this Graph? (catchy headline)

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

1.From looking at the graphs I can see that there are differences for each. For instance the first graph displays misshapen states that are different sizes to emphasize how some states have a higher impact than others. The blocks are also the corresponding number of electoral votes each state has. While the second graph shows a more traditional view of the states. The first graph also shows the small amount that either Trump or Biden won in Maine and Nebraska while the second graph has this off to the side. 

2.I wonder about why the graph number two, or the standard model, is the most frequently used model. I feel as though some people would understand the number of votes each state has if it were in a visual representation as graph number two. I also wonder why Maine and Nebraska have two or three different parts to it.

3.Since New Hampshire is a swing state we could go either way. We are small and on the lower end of the number scale for electoral votes but that isn’t a bad thing because sometimes these swing states can sway the election and potentially help one candidate win.

4.The graphs both show results of the 2020 election in different ways. A catchy headline would be: “Standard of new? Should we change from a standard map to a new one to better understand the country's presidential voting style?”

The bottom map shows each state that red or blue has won and not the amount of votes each counts towards. You could say they were showing, "The vote of each state."

raw_comment:
I notice that the first map shows sizes the states in proportion to how many electoral votes they have, with each cube representing one vote. There is clearly more blue shown than red, which aligns with the actual result of the election. The second graph, on the other hand, simply shows each state as it appears normally on a map. Here there is a higher volume of red than blue, contrary to the election results. 
I wonder whether the second map has misled people into thinking the election was closer than it is, or if it caused people to make the argument of “more land is red, so Trump should have won.” I also wonder why maps like the first one, which accurately display the voting power of each state, are rarely used even though they convey the data more accurately.
The difference between these two graphs truly shows me and my community how the physical size of a state doesn’t matter when it comes to electoral power. As someone from New Hampshire, it’s fascinating to look at the first map and see our tiny state portrayed as bigger than Alaska, the largest state in the US.
These graphs show the disparity between land size and electoral votes, as well as the voter demographics across our country. Just by looking at them we can infer that people living in areas of high population density such as cities tend to vote Democrat, while those living in more rural areas tend to vote Republican. An idea for a headline would be “Land Doesn’t Vote, People Do.”

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the first graph shows each state as a group of boxes. Each box represents one of the states’ electoral votes. This allows the viewer to understand how much influence each state has on the election because every states’ size is determined by the number of electoral votes it has. The second graph  shows the geographical area of each state, which makes it difficult to discern how much impact each state has on the election.

2. I wonder why the most common graph used by news outlets to reflect election results is the graph that shows the geographical size of each state. These graphs can cause confusion because they are usually mostly red, giving the impression that the republican candidate won the election even when they did not. This is because they fail to show that although there are fewer blue states, many have larger populations and more electoral votes than republican states. Graphs that show each states’ number of electoral votes clearly convey this information, so they should be used instead.

3. These graphs show what areas voted for which candidate, which helps us determine if we are living in a generally liberal or conservative area. For example, I can understand from this graph that I live in a generally liberal region of the United States because the state I live in and many of the surrounding states are blue.

4. Both of these graphs reflect the 2020 election results by showing which candidate won each state.

A Tale of Two Graphs
