## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
After observing both graphs, I noticed the effect the two colors had on my eyes. The red coloring was deceiving, especially in the second graph. When I observed the first graph, I had an easier time identifying that blue had the majority of the votes. I could look at each state and tell that there were more blue states than red states. Having the states separated and not touching was a major help when identifying the winner. When I looked at the second graph, the red color stood out. It looked as if red held the majority of the votes. 
I wonder why the red coloring has this effect on my eyes. I did not have a problem observing the first graph but I did with the second. All the red seemed to blend together and looked as if it was the majority. 
If other observers share the same issues I had while reading the second graph, my community including me could easily confuse the winner of the 2020 election. Reading a graph incorrectly can cause a negative impact throughout a community. People may look at the second graph as I did and confuse the winners. A community could become very confused and separated over a graph like the second one. It gives the correct results but presents them in a misleading way. One person may read the graph correctly and one person may not. This could cause a feud between these two people or even a whole community. 
A new headline that captures the maps’ main idea is the deceiving red.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the first map shows the number of electoral votes for each state, which shows how important each state is to the outcome of the election. It shows all the states spread apart, making it obvious that Biden won most of the states. In each state there are small boxes that represent the amount of electoral votes that state has. So, the size of those states do not correspond to the actual size in real life. On the other hand, the second map shows which state sides with which party. This map makes it seem like Trump won because more of the United States is colored red. This map doesn’t show the electoral votes for each state so to the eye it is inaccurate on who won the election because the central states have less electoral votes then the coastal states. 
2. When looking at the first map I wonder why Nebraska and Maine have both red and blue boxes? I also wonder why some of the states are slightly darker blue than others?
3. This impacts my community because we live in such a small state with a relatively small population yet we have a similar amount of electoral votes as other larger states. It also shows who we gave our electoral votes to, and in our case New Hampshire gave our votes to Biden. 
4.The first map represents the states size’s with their electoral votes and the second map represents the states with their normal size and the color of the candidate they gave their electoral votes to. “Land Area vs. Population”

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
When analyzing the two displays, I noticed several different things.  The most prominent is that the graphs attempt to portray different things.  The first values data over looks, specifically, it shows the number of electoral votes for each state instead of the correct shape and cleanliness of the state.  The second graph takes a more traditional approach, and shades states in with whichever color it sided with.  I’m interested in the first graph since it takes an unorthodox approach to presenting the information.  
Since electoral votes are based on the population of a state, I wonder if each vote is directly proportional to a percentage of the state.  For example, if one of New Hampshire’s votes represents more or less people than say for one of California’s votes.  
Since we live in a relatively small state with a low population, I’m not surprised with our electoral college votes compared to our state size.  It appears that we are on the lower end of states when considering electoral college votes, but that isn’t necessarily a bad thing.
Since the first graph appears to present data more accurately, I would question the authenticity or effectiveness of the second graph in a title comparing the two.  A catchy title that I came up with could be “Has looking simple ruined our perception of an efficient display of information?”

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:

  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

|---|---|---|

| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment: One thing I noticed was how the first map demonstrates what states voted for what candidates by showing how many electoral college votes each state has. The second map just shows the US and which states voted for who. Also, the states with a larger population voted blue, while those with less people voted red. This is why states like California and New York voted for Biden. On both maps, it shows flip states in a shaded color, and you can see that all the flip states voted blue in this election. I wonder why Nebraska and Maine each have one electoral vote for the other candidate. This information impacts me because I live in the United States, so the laws and changes that the President makes can effect my everyday life positively or negatively.

raw_comment:
1.) Generally, democrat strongholds tend to be located in densely populated areas. We have seen states like California with the highest populations going overwhelmingly blue that contain massive cities like Los Angeles or New York. Both of these states vote blue by a longshot and are both coastal states. States like Washington, Oregon, and New Jersey are also densely populated areas on coastal areas that tend to vote blue. However, two states with large populations, Texas and Florida voted red this election. What I found interesting was that the democrats were able to win states like Wisconsin, Michigan, and Georgia which were previously red. This made me wonder why these states went blue this election, whether COVID played a role, and what the democrats did that the republicans did not.

2.) What are some policies that encapsulate densely populated areas and shift these communities to vote blue?  The Midwest does not nearly make as much of the population up as these cities, yet makes 2/3 of the land and tends to be mostly red. Where does this polarization between densely populated and rural areas spur from?

3.) Josh Gottheimer, who is my congressman, has a history of working across the aisle to ensure that people get necessary social programs but the economic stability of the region remains unaffected. I am not surprised by these election results and I believe that life goes on.

4.) A Tale of Two Backgrounds: The Increasing Polarization of Rural and Urban Areas

  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? 
I notice that the first map is way more block-like, and is more based on population to determine the size of the shape. The way its designed also reminds me of if the USA was made to look like the periodic table, with all the states being block-like, similar to how elements are on the periodic table. 

2. What do you wonder?
Why are Maine and Nebraska the only states that base their votes on districts rather than using the Electoral college system? What if they followed the same trend all of the other 48 states followed? How about vice versa? What if they were the only states not to do district counts? Why are the midwestern state the only unpredictable states.


3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
The impact this has on me and my community is that, for Ohio, it shows how much of a mixed bag Ohio is, given this election and its voting history. it can go blue like in 2008, or it can go red, like in 2020

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps' main idea.

What's going on in both maps, is that it's showing Biden won the election, but what's unique about the first graph is that it shows bigger states aren't more populated, in fact, they're usually the complete opposite. 
I would title the headline "The population of a state doesn't equal size in an election", referring to that first map.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
At first glance of the map, I noticed that Joe Biden was able to win the 2020 election by a fairly large margin. He was able to flip and win battleground states like GA, PA, MI, AZ, NV, and WI. What also lead to his victory was the fact that he was able to keep control and win the states that typically go blue like NY and CA. Lastly, Biden put himself in a solid position for himself ( or another democratic representative) in 2024, by closing gaps in FL, TX, and NC.

A few things I am wondering about is what happened in the states that Biden was able to flip. What resonated well with the people that he was able to change the minds of. 

I live in an area of NY that typically votes, and goes blue for all major votes, meaning that my life won't change all that much. This year's graph further shows how NY is a "blue" state.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the first map is broken down into blocks that seem to represent electoral votes, and the second is just by state. Only two states in the first map aren't solidly one color-- Nebraska and Maine -- because they split electoral votes instead of letting the winner take all.
2. I wonder what the map would look like if more states split electoral votes like Maine and Nebraska -- would the election have been closer?
3. My community is a blue bubble inside of typically-Republican Ohio, so seeing it go red twice in a row for Donald Trump is almost like a shock to the community. It showed me and people in my city that we're a tiny group inside of our overall red state. 
4. What went on in the 2020 election? An electoral vs. state breakdown

raw_comment:
1. I notice that when looking at the second graph, if one didn't know what the electoral college was they would surely think that the republican candidate won the election because more states appear red.
2. I wonder why certain states commonly vote republican or democrat. Just how big is the pressure in these states in young voters to vote for a specific party just because of tradition.  Do people in these states think more for themselves or for the reputation of their state.
3. I live in Ohio, my state is red, but where in Ohio I'm from, a Cleveland suburb, is very blue and tends to vote blue in elections. I don't feel as though Ohio being red represents the bigger metropolitan areas. There is a huge divide in political beliefs in my state, the more rural the area you're in the more republican and conservative the ideals are. It's quite the opposite for our urban neighborhoods. 
4. "The division of America, a look into the 2020 primary election"

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that most of the states that we would normally consider "republican" Trump was able to win (those in the mid-West and South). But, on the Electoral College votes winner-map, we are able to see the distribution of votes is not always overwhelmingly for one candidate. We are able to see in Nebraska and Maine there is one small box in the state that actually went the other way (in Nebraska it went blue, in Maine it went red). This displays clearly the idea of winner-takes-all in most American states, outside of the very few exceptions like Nebraska and Maine, who stand out for not having just one color or another.
2. I wonder if it is likely that the first map could be used more often if the Electoral System was either abolished or strongly reformed. Each state would then have a chance to have different winners per "block" in their state, possibly giving way to more diverse opinions and a more fair system of voting in president. I also wonder why states in the mid-West so strongly associate with Trump, even though many of Trump's policies hurt working-class men and women. In many of these states, the very people voting for Trump are most likely negatively affected by his politics. 
3. Once again, Ohio went red during this election. Ohio is considered a swing-state, meaning that the results in our state and my community is very important to the presidential race. Voting in my community and state is therefore very important.
4. "Winner Takes All: Biden Wins"

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

Florida and Texas are getting less and less red due to the diversifying populations there. Also, the intellectual urban centers of the blue collar swing states overwhelmed the rural red areas, except for Ohio.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the easternmost and westernmost parts of the country are strictly blue states, while the middle of the country tends to vote red.  It seems that traditionally blue states voted for their historical party preferences. On the other hand, key swing states--like Arizona and Georgia--voted Democrat in this election instead of Republican. The first map shows a more accurate representation of the results, as a glance at the second map shows an overwhelming amount of red.
2. I wonder why rural areas tend to vote Republican and what policies these voters anticipated Trump to help them with? Also, I wonder why this phenomenon occurs in every election cycle? Why does the second map seem to show more red than the first, despite a Democrat victory in both?  
3. Biden’s victory will have a major impact on my community. The Northeast’s tendency to vote blue has instilled progressive policies in New Hampshire, shaping the Seacoast community to be liberal. In regards to the coronavirus, Biden’s victory signifies an upcoming change to our country’s pandemic response. Since my community is a traditionally blue area, we will most likely adopt Biden’s new ideas, whether that means mandatory vaccinations or a mask mandate. 
4. “Biden Emerges Victorious Despite Polarization Throughout the United States”

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the nation is quite literally divided in their electoral choices- both the east and west coast are primarily blue, whereas the midwest and middle swath of the USA is predominantly red. 
2. Connecting back to my response to the first question, I wonder why this is- why are the coasts mainly democratic, while the middle states are mostly republican?
3. Wisconsin was a key swing state, and Biden managed to flip it, which was critical to his win. Parts of Wisconsin, like Madison, are more liberal, and so it has a large impact on my community. 
4. These graphs each show similar things, but do it in different ways. The first one easily depicts the electoral vote situation, whereas the other shows areas won better. It's important to realize what the maps show to help understand the results. The top graph clearly shows that Biden won with the electoral system, while the other looks more like the Republicans have the majority, which is not actually the case. A catchy title might be "2020 election in numbers - not area."

raw_comment:
1.  While looking at the two maps, I noticed that the more typical map which shows the winner by state at a glance looks largely Republican. In the other map, the one showing the winner by electoral college vote, that one seemed to be largely Democratic. 

2. After seeing the large difference in the two maps, I wonder why the most commonly used and most often referenced map is the one showing the winner by state, whereas the most accurate map giving the best representation of the population is the map giving the winner by electoral college vote.

3. This impacts me because I feel as though not everyone knows how the current election map is not an accurate representation of my community, as the electoral college vote map allows states to be accurately represented not based on land mass, but population density. The map will then show the country did not actually vote Republican

4. One specific difference I saw between the two maps was that larger states, like Alaska, are a fraction of their size on the electoral college map, as some of the larger states have a smaller population density then others. A catchy headline would be, By State, or by Vote?

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
I noticed that the first graph represents states with blocks and each block equals 1 electoral vote. For example, Montana is made up of 3 blocks and is given 3 electoral votes. I also noticed that there is more blue and this would be accurate given that Joe Biden won more electoral votes then President Trump. On the second graph, which is a political map (pun intended), there is more red which may seem misleading. However, because the Electoral Collage is based on population not area this map is also accurate. On both graphs I noticed that won more states along both coasts whereas President Trump won more states in the middle of the Continental US.
I wonder why Joe Biden generally won the states along the coasts that mostly have more major cities opposed to the less densely populated mid-western states.
This has a positive impact on my community and me because the majority of my county, my state, and my nation voted for Joe Biden. Although many people did not vote for him the majority of Americans did therefore it has a positive impact because the President the majority of my community wanted was elected.
In the first graph which represents the Electoral Collage is mostly blue given that the majority of the population voted for Joe Biden. The second graph that shows the geographical US is red because this map does not take into account population and many states with a lower population per square mile ratio voted for Trump. A catchy headline is "306 to 232 a Nation ÷ed"

raw_comment:
A) I noticed that the top map displays the Maine and Nebraska split electoral college votes next to the other electoral college votes from those states, whereas the bottom map includes them off to the side. The top map shows each electoral college vote as one square, whereas the bottom map just colors the whole state. I think that the top map is better for representing those aforementioned split electoral college votes from the two states who do the EC a bit differently from the rest.
B) I wondered why some states had a darker shade of blue than others. It seems that a darker blue represents a state that flipped from voting Republican in 2016 to Democrat in 2020, such as Pennsylvania or Arizona. Looking at the map keys confirmed this idea.
C) New Hampshire is pretty small geographically compared to most states, but the top map makes it clear that the Granite State has a similar amount of electoral college votes as many other states. Still, relative to most other states, New Hampshire remains pretty small, both in population and size.
D) I have devised two hopefully attention-grabbing headlines:
 - Top Map: “Land Doesn’t Vote: Electoral College Votes Visualized”
 - Bottom Map: “A Divided America: Voter Preference from Each State Visualized”

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the Republican votes are generally more centralized in the middle of the country and Democratic votes are more on the coastlines. I also notice that the votes are more accurately represented in the first map than the second one, showing votes based on population instead of land.
2. I wonder if people would understand the electoral college and population density better if the second map was used more frequently, or if that would cause more confusion because it looks unusual.
3. This impacts me and my community because it can show in a visual way how the electoral college works, which may help others understand how even if the country is mostly red looking at the second map, it doesn't mean the population votes mostly Republican.
4. This first map shows how states vote with equally sized boxes representing the electoral votes each state has. This can clear up some confusion as to why there are so many large red states which take up a large portion of the map, yet Trump did not win the election. A headline that captures this map's main idea can be "America As Its Electoral Votes."

  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

raw_comment: I noticed that the two graphical displays highlight how bias and misleading appearances are used in politics. In the first graph, the voting results are shown in accordance to the state population, whereas, in the second graph, the results are shown with colors according to the proportion of the state land. ## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
1. In the first graph, it shows each state sectioned off by its number of electoral college votes and which party won those respected votes. In the second graph it shows each state's winner. The top graph is not geographically correct as its focus is on the electoral college votes, while the bottom graph is far more aesthetically pleasing to look at and examine. 
2. I wonder if more people would prefer the top map over the bottom map. Although it is technically more accurate and in-depth, do people prefer simplicity over more knowledge?
3. Using the results of this election, my community has seen that Ohio is no longer a swing state and is becoming a red state. 
4.  These maps show how each state voted in the presidential election, with the top map splitting it up by electoral college votes and the bottom map by who won each state. A catchy headline could be "Trump Suffers a Case of the Biden Blues."

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

1. I notice that the top map is much more representative of the population than the area of the state. Montana, Wyoming, North Dakota, South Dakota all look very small because they have a low population, when they are actually quite large in size. 

2. I wonder why we don't use maps like the top one more in mainstream media to show the results of the election. Electoral votes, not area of the state, depict the voting power a state has. So at a glance a map depicting the electoral college votes is much more accurate.

In this election,voted red but the blue party won the majority. This shows that Ohio is shifting away from being a swing state, and towards being a red state. 

4. The graph shows how the electoral college voted in the 2020 election. A catchy titie could be "America Now"

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

1. In this map representing the election, it's more of a block-like representation of the election, with each state separated rather than put together like a puzzle. The map also gives a representation of each size of the state (by population), which is how the electoral map is counted... 

2. What would the map look like if you put all the block states together like the United States? How would it compare in size to the actual map? 

3. The impact this has on my community is that even though our community (Lakewood) tends to be more Democrat, Ohio as a whole is red (Republican), this is mostly due to rural areas in Ohio. So basically, our community is just one piece of the puzzle within a puzzle piece. 

4. Besides the graph representing that Joe Biden won the election, it also represents the true population size of these states, especially states that are big in size, but small in population (like Alaska and the Dakotas). A Catchy title could be "What would the United States look like as if they were sized down to represent population"

- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.

raw_comment:
Notice - The first thing that I noticed in the top graph is that not only are the number of electoral votes are represented, but we are also shown which parts of each states tend to be more republican or democratic. Whereas the bottom graph is showing more of an "overall" outcome rather than breaking it down. For example, in the top graph Nebraska was primarily republican, but it also shows the small section that voted for Biden. 

Wonder - I wonder if having these two graphs somewhat helped people understand the outcomes of this election if they were apart of the group that essentially were weary of the winner. 

Impact - This graph ultimately shows that in a time of need, people will rise to vote and further better their country for the future. Over the past four years people have seen what our government has done and have decided what need to happen next and have selected a candidate who will support them. 

Going On - In each of these graphs, we are being shown which states were won by the election candidates whether it was for the republican party or the democratic. The difference is that the top half is showing each states broken down to the size of their electoral votes. Catchy Title "The Distorted Divide"

- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
I noticed three things. The first thing is the graph above is more reflective of electoral power. Very large states where no one lives in them are small and inconsequential on this map. Secondly both maps are deceiving especially the above one. Since the above map looks like it's divided into districts it appears as if all districts went a certain way. Thirdly This above map makes the United States look more balanced. On the original map it seems like 70% of the country is red. The new map makes the country look more 50/50.

I wonder if moves will be made by either party to get their people to live in opposite states or districts to try and flip them.

It means that Lakewood Ohio is the blue bubble in a sea of red. This is due to gerrymandering and a stacked republican state government.

The thing with this graph is it is showing a more reflective map of the country. "The Political Landscape of the Real America" This is my tagline and it is epic.

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
