sentence_classifications.image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.

- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.

raw_comment:
1. What I notice first about these maps is how they differ: One is based on electoral votes, representing each state by the number of votes it has in the electoral college. The second is purely geographical, showing the party that took said state overall. 
2. I wonder why, even in the map that represents electoral votes, the republican areas seem larger. Knowing the Democrats took the popular vote, it seems strange that such vast ae=reas of the continent are represented as red. 
3. The impact that this has on my community directly is rather large because I live in a very densely populated and Democratic area within Ohio. Watching the electoral college of the state I call my own tip away from my values can be daunting for myself and my community.
4. These maps both represent the 2020 election results, representing the two main parties on a state-by-state basis. A headline for this could be: A Visual Representation of The Electoral College in The United States

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

What’s going on: The top graph is organized by the state’s number of electoral votes. That’s why it seems kinda distorted as a lot of people have noticed. Most of the voters voted for Biden, but there is one that voted Trump.

What I wonder: I wonder why some big states like Alaska have so few electoral votes. Is it determined by the population of that state in general?

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:

  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

|---|---|---|

| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |

| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |

| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

What do you notice?

The top graph of today’s article further decomposes voting statistics based off of absolutely blue (Biden) states, flip sorta states for either side, and those completely red (Trump). 



What do you wonder? 

I wonder if the New York Times presented readers with  two graphs in order to satisfy those who enjoy scrutinizing the most minor details on political maps. As well as providing generalized election results for people searching for a simple information blanket. Also, what exactly makes certain states swing or flip ones?  After researching more, I was able to discover these "swing states" are usually identified as such because of possessing closely divided political populations. 



What impact does this have on you and your community?

Whoever strides forward as President and VP will serve as a broader voice for my country, in addition to displaying the type of character voters deem fit enough for high status in our government.



What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.



We are viewing the United States’s political placement on the 2020 election, incorporating state’s electoral college votes with their selected candidates, and those that can flip either Democratic or Republican. A possible headline could be, "Democratic, Republican, and everything in between".

raw_comment:
I notice that in the first graph it shows the number of Electoral College votes by winner, and in the second graph, it shows each state’s winner. In the first graph, I notice that many key states flipped to President-elect Biden. This information is also illustrated in the second graph. In the first graph, each state is broken down into specific areas to show the types of Electoral voters. In the second graph, it shows the U.S. map with all of the states in their usual places. The second map also shows which states won, in terms of if it’s Democrat or Republican. 

I wonder why a specific color pattern has to represent that a state switched. If a state switched, shouldn’t it be represented with the color it switched to and not a color showing it switched from one color to another one?

The color of my state, Texas, impacts me and my community because it reflects the Republican ideas people are most interested in. Because Texas is a red state, the majority of people want it to reflect the ideas of a Republican leader. The people ultimately want the leader to influence the surrounding areas. 

A catchy title would be: The Primary Colors of Voting

raw_comment: The map displays the outcome of the 2020 presidential election. Joe Biden won with 306 electoral votes and Donald Trump with only 232. The first map gives you more of an idea of how many electoral votes each state got. The states are divided almost into sections. The states on the East and West coast are mostly Democratic and the mid states tend to be more Republican. I wonder what percent of the population each state voted and it would be nice to show the overall population of each state as well. I live in a predominately democratic city, making it unfortunate for my city that my state is red. This discouraged a lot of people in my area. However, Joe Biden still won the overall vote. As for a catchy headline, I would recommend "Maps of Perhaps the Most Controversial U.S. Presidential Election"

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

|---|---|---|

| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

raw_comment:
1. In this map representing the election, it's more of a block-like representation of the election, with each state separated rather than put together like a puzzle. The map also gives a representation of each size of the state (by population), which is how the electoral map is counted...

2.  What would the map look like if you put all the block states together like the United States? How would it compare in size to the actual map? 

3. The impact this has on my community is that even though our community (Lakewood) tends to be more Democrat, Ohio as a whole is red (Republican), this is mostly due to rural areas in Ohio. So basically, our community is just one piece of the puzzle within a puzzle piece. 

4. Besides the graph representing that Joe Biden won the election, it also represents the true population size of these states, especially states that are big in size, but small in population (like Alaska and the Dakotas).

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |
